newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Fresh falls seen for prices.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Fresh falls seen for prices.

text.p: Precious metals markets opened the new year breaking to the downside, leading dealers to forecast further losses this week.
"Historically the first few days of a new year have set the tone for the first quarter, so it looks like weakness is set to continue for the moment," one senior bullion dealer said.
On Friday afternoon gold was fixed at $364.00 per ounce, its lowest fix since $363.00 on November 3, 1993, compared with $366.55 last Thursday.
But a fresh wave of selling largely on New York's Comex market pressured gold to a close of $361.90/$362.40.
Market participation was still thin after the holiday period, which might have exaggerated the price weakness, dealers said.
"Physical demand is there but it tends to be cute in some places. These people will know to hold off buying for now to see if they can get in at lower prices later," a dealer said.
Some dealers were now looking for gold to probe as low as $360 per ounce, a value not seen since early October 1993.
"After that it's a parachute job," one dealer said, adding that the investment fund portfolios were positioned to take advantage of weaker prices.

"It's not clear that there is enough fresh news in the market to replace the bearish psychology which prevailed before Christmas," said bullion market analyst Tony Warwick-Ching at research group CRU International.
"The tone is still bearish," one dealer said, while another referred to "gold's bearish internal combustion" as overwhelming any positive influence for the moment.

Part of the gloom came from the threat to the gold market from possible central bank selling, especially in Europe, where the banks were re-assessing their largely dormant and non-revenue earning gold reserves, several analyst said.
"Producer selling and central bank selling in response to a price rally will stop gold and silver going above their historic highs (in 1997)," one said.
Industrial precious metals users were expected to start returning to the market this week but that was unlikely to change the outlook.
"Physical buying may slow the fall but the market will not turn round until the speculators begin to buy instead of sell," a dealer said.
The other precious metals were also lower, fatigued and likely to follow gold.
